slides.title: Complex housing reduces repetitive behavior
body: **Stereotypy** is repetitive behavior with little variation and no obvious immediate goal. Bailoo and colleagues recorded female C57 and SWISS mice in barren, nesting-only, enriched, or super-enriched housing. Video scoring expressed stereotypy as a proportion of active time, separating repetition from simple inactivity.

The super-enriched condition connected two cages and provided shelters, climbing opportunities, tunnels, and regularly changed objects. Stereotypy was greatly reduced in both strains compared with the other conditions; nesting material or modest enrichment did not produce a consistent equivalent reduction.

The result links a substantial change in living conditions to reduced behavioral pathology. It does not establish that every repetitive act reflects the same experience, or that a mouse without visible stereotypy has good welfare. Behavioral expression depends on the opportunities available in the enclosure.

slides.title: Mice actively use opportunities in complex cages
body: **Environmental enrichment** supplies resources that allow more species-typical activity than basic food, water, and bedding alone. In the same experiment, mice were scored as engaged when they contacted an enrichment item or manipulated the housing environment, including bedding in barren cages.

Mice in the super-enriched condition engaged with their environment during more than 85% of observed intervals on average. Barren-housed mice engaged least, while nesting and enriched cages supported intermediate levels. The comparison therefore measures use of resources rather than their mere presence.

Contact with objects is not a direct measure of pleasure. Shelter use can also obscure behavior from an observer, and engagement combines resting inside a shelter with active manipulation. Resource provision should be evaluated alongside repetitive behavior and other outcomes rather than treated as an automatically effective label.

slides.title: Hormone responses depend on mouse strain
body: **Glucocorticoids** are adrenal hormones involved in the physiological response to stress; corticosterone is a major rodent glucocorticoid. Bailoo and colleagues measured its fecal metabolites, products formed after hormone processing, to compare endocrine outcomes without taking blood during the measurement.

SWISS mice in barren and nesting-only cages had higher metabolite concentrations than mice in enriched and super-enriched cages. C57 mice did not exhibit the same consistent housing effect. Concentrations were reported in ng per 0.05 g of feces, and excretion reflects secretion delayed by approximately 8–10 hours.

The collections followed cage changes, so the measurements partly reflect responses to husbandry. A lower metabolite value cannot be equated with uniformly lower distress, and a housing effect in one genetic background need not generalize to another. Behavioral and endocrine measures describe related but distinct biological processes.

slides.title: Different welfare measures can disagree
body: **Perseveration** is inappropriate persistence in a response pattern when changing responses would be useful. Mice completed a two-choice guessing task in which reward probabilities depended on their preceding choices. This assessed inhibitory control separately from home-cage stereotypy.

Housing condition and stereotypy level did not consistently predict the perseveration score. A separate spatial judgment task trained mice to approach a rewarded location and withhold approach at a nonrewarded location, then tested three intermediate locations. Enrichment did not cause a consistent shift toward approaching ambiguous cues across both strains.

These negative results coexist with reduced stereotypy in super-enriched cages. They limit the inference that one visible improvement necessarily normalizes every cognitive outcome. A welfare assessment supported by several independent measurements is less dependent on the assumptions of any single behavioral task.

slides.title: Full social contact predicts less macaque stereotypy
body: Gottlieb and colleagues assessed captive rhesus macaques using 5-minute behavioral observations over 11 years. **Motor stereotypies** were repeated whole-body movements such as pacing, rocking, and somersaulting. Housing categories distinguished solitary cages, protected contact through bars, and full access to a social partner.

Full-contact pair housing was associated with less stereotypy than either solitary housing or protected contact. The protected-contact partition had bars 4.5 cm apart but did not provide the same association with reduced stereotypy. Foraging devices were also associated with a lower likelihood of stereotypy when present.

The study controlled analytically for measured individual differences and repeated observations, but housing was not randomly assigned. The findings support providing meaningful social and foraging opportunities while leaving open the influence of selection into different housing conditions. Visual contact alone was not equivalent to full social access in this population.

slides.title: Temperament predicts stereotypy expression
body: **Behavioral inhibition** describes withdrawal from unfamiliar situations. After observing stereotypy, investigators presented a novel food item and recorded inspection for 3 minutes. Macaques inspecting within 5 seconds were classified as bold; later inspection was moderate, and no inspection was inhibited.

Bold and moderate responders were more likely to express motor stereotypy than inhibited responders. The association remained in a model that also included housing, enrichment, rearing history, ancestry, and age. A visibly active monkey and a withdrawn monkey can therefore express an adverse environment differently.

The novel-object response is an operational measure of temperament rather than a diagnosis. Absence of pacing in an inhibited individual does not by itself establish favorable welfare. Conversely, the association does not prove that bold temperament causes pathology; shared developmental influences could contribute to both behaviors.

slides.title: Early rearing predicts later repetitive behavior
body: The macaque analysis also classified the environment experienced during the first 6 months of life. Outdoor corral rearing provided a large social group, while other categories included sheltered groups, indoor groups, nursery rearing, and indoor mother rearing. These histories differed before the adult observations began.

Nursery-reared and indoor mother-reared monkeys had the highest modeled risk of motor stereotypy, whereas corral-reared animals had the lowest. Current housing and foraging conditions were included alongside early history, so the analysis did not attribute every adult difference to the cage occupied at observation.

Developmental history can influence the later expression of behavioral pathology and the apparent response to husbandry. These observational associations cannot identify a unique developmental mechanism or separate every correlated feature of rearing. They also mean that identical present-day cages need not produce identical behavior in animals with different past experiences.

slides.title: Captivity changes hormone responses in wild birds
body: Lattin and colleagues followed wild house sparrows during 4 weeks of laboratory captivity. **Baseline corticosterone** was sampled within 3 minutes of capture or room entry; the acute stress response was sampled after 30 minutes of standardized restraint. These measurements distinguish resting hormone levels from a response to challenge.

Baseline corticosterone rose after 2 weeks relative to capture. Restraint-induced concentrations depended on both time in captivity and life-history stage, including moult, winter, and breeding. Birds also lost body mass during captivity, while recorded behaviors changed over the same period.

Initial lower baseline hormone levels and stronger acute responses predicted some more favorable feeding or behavioral outcomes. A large challenge response is therefore not automatically evidence of poor coping. The observational design relates physiological variation to captivity responses without proving that altering corticosterone would reproduce those outcomes.

slides.title: PET measures dopamine binding in sparrow striatum
body: **Dopamine** is a transmitter that modifies neural signaling through several receptor classes. The **striatum** is a forebrain region involved in behavior and action selection. Investigators used positron emission tomography, or PET, to localize a radioactive ligand that binds dopamine D2 receptors in living sparrows.

The ligand, carbon-11 raclopride, accumulated more strongly in striatum than in the cerebellar reference region. Giving haloperidol at 0.5 mg/kg displaced striatal binding during a scan, supporting the interpretation that the signal included receptor-specific binding rather than only nonspecific tracer distribution.

**Binding potential** estimates available specific binding relative to a reference region. It is not a direct count of receptors and can depend on receptor availability and competition from endogenous dopamine. PET therefore connects neurochemical organization to captivity responses while retaining important limits on what a change in signal means.

slides.title: Dopamine binding changes with captivity and season
body: Sparrows underwent a first D2-receptor PET scan 24 hours after capture, with a subset scanned again after 4 weeks. Striatal binding potential decreased in moulting birds, while comparable decreases were not detected in winter or breeding birds. The neural response to captivity therefore differed by life-history stage.

Larger declines in binding were associated with more feather ruffling and beak wiping during captivity. Higher initial binding predicted more feeding at early assessments but lower body mass later, so receptor binding did not track every behavioral and physiological endpoint in the same direction.

These associations are consistent with dopamine-related changes contributing to captivity responses, but do not establish receptor loss or a human psychiatric disorder. The first scan was already after capture, so it was not an undisturbed wild baseline. A seasonal, individual, and temporal interpretation is needed before using PET as a welfare marker.

slides.title: Repeated restraint increases neuronal firing gain
body: Rosenkranz and colleagues restrained male rats for 20 minutes on 7 days within a 9-day period; controls received comparable handling without restraint. Intracellular recordings then measured **excitability**, the number of action potentials elicited by a controlled input, in principal neurons of the lateral amygdala.

Current pulses lasted 800 milliseconds. Firing gain increased from 0.68 to 1.55 action potentials per 100 pA in repeatedly stressed rats. A single restraint session did not produce the same increase. **Action potentials** are brief regenerative electrical signals, so greater gain means more neural output for comparable injected current.

The increase persisted when neurons were held at −70 mV, limiting an explanation based solely on different resting voltages. These recordings establish a cellular effect of repeated restraint under anesthesia, not a direct measurement of conscious fear or the effects of every captive environment.

slides.title: Resting membrane changes do not explain all stress effects
body: **Input resistance** describes how strongly a neuron’s membrane voltage changes for a small injected current. Repeatedly stressed rats had increased input resistance in lateral-amygdala neurons, and the membrane time constant was longer, indicating a changed response to subthreshold inputs that do not trigger spikes.

However, matching voltage and examining these passive properties did not account for the full increase in spike output. Blocking fast inhibitory inputs through GABA-A-related chloride conductances also left a stress-related excitability difference. **GABA-A receptors** are transmitter-gated channels that contribute to rapid inhibitory signaling in this preparation.

These controls separate a change in intrinsic spike regulation from a simple loss of the tested inhibitory input. They do not establish that inhibition is unchanged throughout the entire intact circuit. Stress can alter several cellular properties simultaneously, while one property remains insufficient to explain the observed firing difference.

slides.title: Stress weakens the brake after a burst of spikes
body: An **afterhyperpolarization** is a period of more negative membrane voltage after spiking that restrains further firing. Calcium entering during activity can activate potassium channels; outward potassium current then contributes to this brake. The medium and slow afterhyperpolarizations were reduced after repeated restraint.

The slow component averaged 2.6 mV in controls and 0.7 mV in stressed rats. Pharmacologically blocking calcium entry reduced the afterhyperpolarization and diminished the excitability difference between groups. These interventions support a calcium-dependent contribution to the stress-related increase in firing.

The results implicate calcium-activated potassium-channel regulation, with small-conductance channels among the candidates. They do not directly identify a lost molecular subtype or quantify channel number. Reduced channel function and altered calcium coupling remain distinct possible mechanisms that the physiological measurements do not fully separate.

slides.title: Enhancing the spike brake reverses hyperexcitability
body: The investigators administered **1-EBIO**, a compound that enhances calcium-activated potassium-channel activity, after recording baseline excitability. At 10 mg/kg it increased the medium afterhyperpolarization and reduced excessive spike output in stressed rats toward the control range. Vehicle-treated animals provided a comparison for injection effects.

slides.title: Early enrichment alters later responses to separation
body: Hegde and colleagues separated rat pups from dams for 3 hours daily between postnatal days 2 and 14. Enriched housing was provided from days 2 through 21, after which treatments ended. Adult testing at days 60–70 compared separation and enrichment in a crossed experimental design.

Pre-weaning enrichment increased adult exploration of the open-field center, while early separation reduced center exploration in standard housing. Total mobility did not differ clearly between separation groups. Adult corticosterone outcomes were also housing-dependent, although endocrine effects were not uniformly eliminated across every comparison.

The long interval between intervention and testing supports developmental consequences rather than only an immediate response to an object. Enrichment combined space, objects, climbing, food variation, and maternal experience, so the study cannot identify a single effective component. The reported outcomes apply to tested adult males, not automatically to both sexes.

slides.title: Early stress and enrichment alter dendritic spines
body: **Dendrites** receive neuronal inputs, and **dendritic spines** are small protrusions that commonly host excitatory synapses. Golgi staining visualized principal neurons in the basolateral amygdala. Investigators counted spines along 60 µm segments of primary and secondary dendrites in adulthood.

Early maternal separation increased spine density under both standard and enriched rearing conditions. Enrichment shifted density downward overall but did not abolish the separation-associated increase. The structural outcome therefore differed from a simple description in which enrichment completely erased every stress effect.

Spine density is a measure of neuronal structure, not a direct recording of synaptic strength or firing. More spines can indicate altered opportunities for input without establishing that each additional spine functions identically. The experiment links developmental conditions to adult anatomy but does not prove that spine changes caused the measured exploration differences.

slides.title: Receptor localization changes without a protein increase
body: A **glucocorticoid receptor**, or GR, is an intracellular receptor whose nuclear localization can influence gene regulation. Investigators immunolabeled GR and identified nuclei with a DNA stain in adult basolateral-amygdala sections. They measured the fraction of nuclei containing detectable GR signal.

Early separation reduced the fraction with nuclear GR, while enrichment had an opposing effect. Total GR protein measured in tissue extracts did not differ clearly across the same treatment comparisons. Receptor location within cells can therefore change without a corresponding detectable increase in overall protein abundance.

The nuclear measurement was made at an endpoint, rather than by following receptor movement live. It supports altered localization but does not directly measure transport speed, receptor activation, or a specific transcriptional consequence. Treating staining overlap as a complete measure of hormone sensitivity would exceed the experiment.

slides.title: Enrichment changes a plasticity-related protein signal
body: **Brain-derived neurotrophic factor**, or BDNF, is a signaling protein associated with neuronal growth and synaptic plasticity. Adult basolateral-amygdala tissue was immunolabeled after the early separation and enrichment treatments. The researchers quantified fluorescence distributions rather than relying only on visible appearance.

Pre-weaning enrichment changed the extent and intensity distribution of BDNF labeling. Separation modified these effects in enriched animals, while some comparisons in standard housing showed no clear difference. A separate tissue-protein assay did not yield the same simple overall enrichment effect across every endpoint.

These results associate early housing with a later molecular environment relevant to plasticity. They do not directly measure BDNF secretion, receptor activation, or the strength of identified synapses. A proposed link between this protein and behavioral resilience remains more tentative than the measured staining differences.

slides.title: A day of isolation changes excitatory synapses
body: Matthews and colleagues isolated mice from cage mates for 24 hours, then recorded identified dopamine neurons in the **dorsal raphe nucleus**, a midbrain region. They measured glutamate-evoked currents through AMPA and NMDA receptors, two receptor classes that support excitatory synaptic signaling.

The AMPA-to-NMDA current ratio increased in dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons after isolation, including when isolation occurred in the familiar home cage. A comparable change was not detected in the sampled ventral-tegmental dopamine neurons. A novel cage without isolation did not reproduce the same increase.

Current rectification and sensitivity to NASPM supported a contribution from calcium-permeable AMPA receptors after isolation. **Rectification** means current flow depends asymmetrically on voltage. These measurements identify a rapid, region-specific synaptic response to social conditions, not a diagnosis of depression or a direct measure of the mouse’s subjective state.

slides.title: Raphe activity tracks reunion after isolation
body: **Fiber photometry** samples fluorescent signals from a population of labeled neurons through an implanted optical fiber. GCaMP6m, a calcium-sensitive fluorescent protein, was expressed in dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons. Calcium changes provided an indirect measure of activity during interactions with another mouse.

After 24 hours of isolation, initial social contact produced larger calcium responses than contact after group housing. The population signal was aligned to interaction bouts, allowing neural responses to be compared with the timing of behavior. The authors also compared responses to a novel object.

The result relates recent social experience to neural responses during reunion. Photometry does not resolve every individual neuron or directly report dopamine release. Increased activity at social contact can reflect a changed motivational state without establishing whether that state has the same subjective character as human loneliness.

slides.title: Raphe dopamine neurons signal to forebrain targets
body: **Optogenetics** uses a light-sensitive protein to control selected neurons. Channelrhodopsin-2, a light-gated cation channel, was expressed in dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons. Blue-light pulses depolarized the cells and evoked action potentials, connecting a defined intervention to neuronal output.

Labeled axons reached the **bed nucleus of the stria terminalis** and the **central amygdala**, forebrain regions involved in behavioral state and threat-related processing. Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, an electrochemical measurement, detected dopamine release in these targets during stimulation with 5-millisecond light pulses.

The combination of labeled projections and evoked transmitter release establishes functional communication from the manipulated cells to these regions. It does not establish that each target mediates the measured social behavior. Artificial synchronous stimulation also differs from the timing and recruitment of neurons during natural social interactions.

slides.title: Dopamine neurons can also release glutamate
body: Dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons were not limited to dopamine transmission. Optical stimulation of their axon terminals evoked rapid **excitatory postsynaptic currents**, electrical currents in target cells driven by excitatory synaptic input. Recordings were made in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis and central amygdala.

A 5-millisecond light pulse evoked short-latency currents recorded at −70 mV. The currents persisted with tetrodotoxin and 4-aminopyridine, a combination used to test direct terminal-mediated transmission, and were consistent with glutamate release. Slower inhibitory responses reflected additional local circuit recruitment.

**Co-transmission** means the same defined neuronal population can signal through more than one transmitter. A behavior caused by manipulating these neurons therefore cannot automatically be attributed to dopamine alone. The experiment establishes glutamatergic signaling from the tested projections without identifying the complete contribution of each transmitter to social motivation.

slides.title: Silencing raphe neurons affects isolated mice differently
body: The investigators expressed halorhodopsin, a light-driven inhibitory protein, in dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons. They compared social preference while the same mice were group-housed and after 24 hours of isolation. Fluorescent-protein controls received light without the inhibitory protein.

Inhibition reduced social preference after isolation but did not produce the same detectable effect in group-housed mice. Spatial heat maps and time in the social zone captured behavior during the task. The circuit’s contribution therefore depended on the preceding social condition.

Separate activation experiments increased social approach but also produced avoidance of a stimulation-associated place. Together, these results distinguish a drive to seek social contact from simple positive reinforcement. They support state-dependent circuit function without proving that chronic isolation, captive primates, or human loneliness share an identical mechanism.

slides.title: Lower fish density does not guarantee better welfare
body: Sen Sarma and colleagues reared zebrafish at 1, 3, or 6 fish/L with barren, gravel, plant, or gravel-plus-plant conditions. **Stocking density** is the number of fish per unit of water volume. Growth, aggression, endocrine responses, and behavior were measured to compare several consequences of these housing conditions.

Fish reared at 1 fish/L were longer and heavier than those at the higher densities. This growth result might appear favorable when considered alone. However, the same low-density groups also expressed more aggression and stronger cortisol release during a group challenge.

Body length in cm and body mass in g describe growth rather than the entire welfare state. Greater size can coexist with greater social conflict. The tested range does not establish that still higher densities are harmless, or that an optimal density can be specified independently of tank structure and social interactions.

slides.title: Sparse zebrafish groups can become more aggressive
body: **Agonistic behavior** includes aggressive acts and related social interactions. During 9 weeks of rearing, observers scored zebrafish strikes, chases, and occasional circling. Comparisons used the same stocking densities and the four physical-enrichment conditions used for growth measurements.

Aggression was higher at 1 fish/L than at 3 or 6 fish/L, with differences emerging across repeated weekly observations. The tested gravel and plant treatments did not produce a clear overall reduction. Merely adding an object was therefore not equivalent to demonstrating a reduction in social conflict.

The findings are compatible with density altering opportunities for stable dominance and repeated pursuit, but do not experimentally isolate that explanation. They also caution against transferring mammalian space-based assumptions directly to schooling fish. What matters biologically includes the pattern of interactions that the available space permits.

slides.title: Group confinement exposes housing-dependent stress
body: **Cortisol** is a principal stress-associated glucocorticoid in zebrafish. To challenge groups, researchers lowered tank water to 1 cm for 30 minutes and then extracted cortisol released into the water. Release was expressed per fish per hour rather than as a blood concentration.

Groups reared at 1 fish/L released more cortisol than groups at 3 or 6 fish/L; the 6 fish/L groups released the least under this challenge. The observed secretion range was 2.7–43.7 ng/fish/h. The tested enrichment conditions did not yield a clear additional effect.

Waterborne release provides a practical group-level endocrine readout, but it combines secretion and transfer into water during a particular challenge. It is not a direct measure of ongoing distress in undisturbed tanks. A lower challenge value also cannot establish favorable welfare without considering aggression and other consequences.

slides.title: Confinement prolongs aggression after crayfish defeat
body: Bacqué-Cazenave and colleagues paired previously isolated, size-matched male crayfish in a confined arena for 20 minutes. Encounters progressed from exploration to fighting, then to continued attacks after one animal retreated. **Social defeat** refers here to the outcome of this observed contest rather than an inferred subjective report.

After defeat, the loser largely stopped fighting while the winner continued approaches and attacks. The loser responded with escapes. The prolonged post-defeat phase differed from mutual fighting, because one animal repeatedly attempted to withdraw while remaining within its opponent’s reach.

The enclosure constrained the separation that a defeated animal might achieve in a larger environment. This offers a concrete mechanism by which captivity can sustain adverse interactions. The experiment measured attacks and escapes directly; describing the sequence as harassment does not establish equivalence to human psychological experience.

slides.title: Defeated crayfish avoid illuminated spaces
body: After pairing, crayfish explored a plus maze containing dark and illuminated arms. **Anxiety-like behavior** was operationalized as stronger light avoidance and more retreats at dark–light boundaries. Winners and previously isolated animals provided comparisons for the defeated animals.

Losers spent about 18% of their time in illuminated arms, compared with about 30% for winners and 32% for isolated controls. The drug chlordiazepoxide increased light-arm exploration in defeated animals, with saline injections controlling for the administration procedure.

The altered behavior after the contest and its pharmacological sensitivity support a persistent defensive state rather than only movements during fighting. They do not independently identify the entire neural pathway or establish the contents of an animal’s experience. Light avoidance must also be distinguished from reduced ability to move.

slides.title: Post-defeat attacks predict later avoidance
body: The pairing observations allowed attacks before and after defeat to be separated. Investigators related the winner’s approaches and attacks to the loser’s later time in illuminated maze arms. This comparison tested whether sustained hostile contact, rather than fighting duration alone, tracked the defensive state.

More attacks during the post-defeat harassment phase were associated with less subsequent light-arm exploration. Duration of fighting did not show the same relationship. Thus, the measured consequence was more closely associated with what happened after withdrawal than with time spent in the initial contest.

The analysis is correlational and cannot exclude other differences between encounters. Nevertheless, it identifies a husbandry-relevant exposure that would be missed by recording only who won. Providing opportunities to escape continued pursuit is a distinct problem from merely reducing the duration of an initial fight.

slides.title: Serotonin contributes to the post-defeat state
body: **Serotonin**, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT, is a transmitter that modulates neural circuits. Brain serotonin was measured after the 20-minute pairing. Concentrations averaged about 236 pg/mg in isolated crayfish, 486 pg/mg in winners, and 691 pg/mg in losers.

Before pairing, methysergide, a broad serotonin-receptor antagonist, was given to the animal expected to lose. Compared with saline controls, treated defeated animals explored illuminated arms more and retreated less. They still lost the contest, separating the defensive state from the act of retreating during defeat.

The pharmacological result supports serotonin-receptor involvement beyond a hormone–behavior association. Whole-brain concentration does not reveal release at a particular synapse, and a broad antagonist does not identify the receptor subtype. The imaged serotonergic neuron comes from a separate motor-circuit preparation, not an identified anxiety circuit.

slides.title: A single serotonin cell modulates a motor network
body: In a separate crayfish study, researchers stimulated an identified serotonergic neuron in the first abdominal ganglion while recording walking-leg motor output. A **ganglion** is a cluster of neuronal cell bodies. Immunostaining and intracellular labeling confirmed that the recorded cell contained serotonin.

Current pulses drove the cell to fire initially at up to 40 Hz, then adapt toward about 17 Hz. Motor neurons in the connected postural network increased, decreased, or maintained their activity during this stimulation. Serotonin therefore did not impose a single uniform direction of motor response.

The isolated preparation retained a leg proprioceptor, a sensory organ that reports limb position, and its central connections. It links transmitter-cell activity to a defined sensorimotor network. It does not directly measure stress experience, and the mixed responses prevent interpreting elevated serotonin as universally excitatory or inhibitory.

slides.title: Serotonin can amplify sensory-driven motor responses
body: A **motor neuron** carries neural output toward muscle, while an **excitatory postsynaptic potential** is a depolarizing response to synaptic input. In some depressor motor neurons, stimulation of the serotonergic cell depolarized the membrane and increased input resistance. The depressor network contributes to downward leg movement.

In the published example, membrane voltage changed from −83.2 to −75.6 mV, and the sensory-driven response increased from about 0.99 to 1.64 mV. Responses to movement of the retained proprioceptor were measured before and during serotonergic-cell stimulation in the same preparation.

The combination of depolarization and greater voltage responsiveness can amplify the effect of sensory input on motor output. Longer-lasting synaptic potentials also contributed. The experiment establishes modulation of a postural circuit; it does not demonstrate that the same cells mediate the defensive state measured in the light–dark maze.

slides.title: The same serotonin input can suppress other neurons
body: Other depressor motor neurons responded to the same identified serotonin-cell stimulation with **hyperpolarization**, a shift to more negative voltage, and reduced input resistance. Sensory-driven responses became smaller rather than larger. These opposing effects occurred within the tested motor system.

In one recorded example, the reflex-related voltage response declined from about 0.077 to 0.045 mV. Synaptic potentials also decayed faster. Reduced voltage responsiveness and a more negative baseline can jointly decrease the influence of a sensory input on the cell’s motor output.

The authors proposed that different receptor locations and local release modes contribute to the opposing effects. These explanations were not a complete molecular identification of the responsible receptors. The results constrain cross-species claims: a rise in a transmitter’s tissue concentration does not specify which neurons or behaviors will be enhanced.

slides.title: Bees learn different outcomes for odor mixtures
body: Bateson and colleagues trained honeybees to distinguish two mixtures of 1-hexanol and 2-octanone. One mixture predicted sucrose; the other predicted a less favorable outcome such as quinine. **Proboscis extension**, extending the feeding mouthparts, served as the measured response rather than locomotor approach.

The rewarded and negative cues used opposite 1:9 and 9:1 mixtures, with three intermediate mixtures presented without reinforcement during testing. These ambiguous odors tested generalization between learned outcomes. After training, experimental bees were shaken for 60 seconds while controls remained undisturbed.

The design compares decisions under uncertainty after a defined acute perturbation. It does not simulate every aspect of chronic captivity. Training establishes the meaning of the odors before the perturbation, helping separate a change in response to learned cues from simply failing to acquire the original discrimination.

slides.title: Acute disturbance biases responses to ambiguous odors
body: A **judgment bias** is a change in how an animal responds to an uncertain cue associated with possible favorable or unfavorable outcomes. Following 60 seconds of shaking, bees were tested within 5 minutes using the trained odors and three intermediate mixtures.

Shaken bees were less likely to extend the proboscis to the negative cue and the intermediate odor nearest it. Responses to the rewarded cue were not detectably reduced. The selective pattern limits an explanation based only on a general inability or unwillingness to extend the feeding mouthparts.

The result supports a disturbance-dependent shift toward unfavorable expectations in this task. It does not provide a subjective report or establish a human-like anxiety disorder. Applying comparable behavioral criteria across taxa requires preserving these experimental controls rather than accepting or rejecting affect solely from the species’ evolutionary position.

slides.title: Bee monoamine changes are not circuit measurements
body: In a separate group of bees, researchers measured **hemolymph**, the circulating fluid of insects, after the same shaking treatment. Dopamine, octopamine, serotonin, and tyramine were assayed. **Octopamine** is a signaling molecule with important roles in insect modulation and reward-related learning.

Around 300 seconds after shaking, dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin concentrations were reduced, whereas tyramine did not show the same clear reduction. The sampling time matched the period when the behavioral tests were performed. These physiological changes accompanied the treatment that altered judgment.

Circulating concentrations are not measurements of transmitter release in an identified brain pathway. The study did not manipulate these monoamines to establish which change caused the behavioral bias. Their direction also differs from elevated brain serotonin after crayfish defeat, because tissue, time, species, and stressor all differ.

slides.title: Octopuses learn places associated with injury
body: Crook tested _Octopus bocki_ in chambers with distinct visual patterns. **Conditioned place avoidance** measures whether an animal later avoids a location associated with an adverse event. Initial preferences were assessed before conditioning, allowing later choices to be compared with each animal’s earlier behavior.

A 0.5% acetic-acid injection in an arm was paired with the initially preferred chamber; saline injection provided a procedural control. On a later free-choice test, acid-treated octopuses reduced their time in the previously preferred chamber compared with controls.

The learned avoidance extends beyond an immediate withdrawal from the injection. It supports an aversive component of the experience but does not independently locate the neural representation or establish every aspect of conscious pain. The study concerns an injury model, not proof that ordinary captivity itself always produces comparable pain.

slides.title: Relief is rewarding specifically after injury
body: **Conditioned place preference** measures increased choice of a context associated with a favorable event. After the acid treatment, Crook paired local lidocaine treatment with the initially nonpreferred chamber. **Local anesthesia** reduces sensory signaling in the treated region rather than necessarily sedating the entire animal.

Octopuses that had received acid later preferred the lidocaine-paired chamber. Animals given saline before lidocaine did not acquire the same preference. This control separates the value of relief from a claim that lidocaine is inherently rewarding regardless of the animal’s preceding state.

Context avoidance after injury and preference for relief provide complementary evidence for an aversive ongoing state. They support an affective interpretation more strongly than withdrawal alone. They do not measure verbalizable feelings or imply that every analgesic procedure, dose, or captive species will have the same outcome.

slides.title: Octopus wound attention persists after the injection
body: **Discriminative pain-related behavior** is behavior directed toward the location or character of an injury. Acid-treated octopuses showed arm grooming, concealment, and skin-removal behavior localized to the injection region. Saline-treated animals did not express the same pattern.

Wound attention persisted for at least 24 hours after the acid injection. Local lidocaine suppressed the observed injury-directed grooming during treatment. The behavior therefore combined spatial specificity, persistence, and sensitivity to a locally acting intervention.

These observations add information beyond place choice: the animal’s response was directed to a particular affected arm. They support an ongoing injury-related state while leaving its full central representation unresolved. A welfare assessment can distinguish persistent wound-directed behavior from generalized activity changes without requiring a human clinical diagnosis.

slides.title: Arm signals remain available to the octopus brain
body: **Nociception** is neural detection and processing of potentially damaging stimulation; it is not identical to subjective pain. Crook recorded activity in the brachial connective, the nerve pathway carrying arm information toward the central brain, before and after local acid injection.

Acid treatment increased ongoing activity and responses to touch in the affected region. Local lidocaine rapidly suppressed ongoing discharge and blocked evoked activity near the injection site. The recorded pathway therefore supplied persistent injury-associated information beyond the arm’s local networks.

Combined with learned avoidance, relief preference, and wound-directed behavior, they strengthen an affective interpretation. Each component addresses a different alternative explanation, which is why the combined evidence exceeds a single withdrawal response.

slides.title: Captivity reshapes cane-toad brain gene expression
body: Yagound and colleagues compared wild-caught cane toads with toads from the same populations maintained in captivity for 7 months. The **transcriptome** is the collection of expressed RNA molecules measured from tissue. Whole-brain RNA sequencing quantified expression rather than recording neuronal activity.

slides.title: Welfare inferences require converging evidence
body: The cane-toad study also measured **expression dispersion**, variation among individuals within a group. Of 155 genes with altered dispersion in range-front toads, 143 varied more among captive animals. The corresponding pattern in range-core toads was less strongly directed toward increased captive variation.

Captivity can therefore change both average expression and individual heterogeneity. These molecular responses accompany the behavioral, endocrine, and cellular effects measured in other taxa, but do not by themselves classify an experience as favorable or unfavorable. Biological change and evidence of harm are related questions that require distinct support.

A comparative welfare judgment is strongest when an environmental exposure, a measured adverse outcome, and a controlled intervention converge. Stereotypy, challenge hormones, neural firing, learned avoidance, and relief preference contribute different evidence. Similarity to humans is not a substitute for these tests, and one absent marker does not establish absence of an adverse state.

items.text: Complex resources reduce mouse stereotypy; full social contact predicts less macaque stereotypy. Different welfare measures can still disagree.
Repeated restraint weakens calcium-dependent afterhyperpolarization and increases lateral-amygdala firing; systemic channel enhancement does not isolate the behavioral site of action.
Raphe dopamine-neuron inhibition reduces social preference after isolation; a neuronal population can also release glutamate.
Fish group and individual cortisol challenges yield different housing effects. Brain serotonin and circulating insect monoamines are different measurements.
Octopus learned avoidance, relief-dependent preference, wound attention, and ongoing afferent signals jointly support an affective injury-related state.
Cane-toad brain expression changes differ by population. Neither a molecular change nor absence of one behavioral marker alone establishes welfare.
